question: Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project record at least 1,000 Mediterranean migrant deaths in 2026 before May 2026?
summary: Ensemble average around 0.54; early-2026 pace (606 deaths by February) makes reaching 1,000 by May plausible, especially if March–April stay elevated.
Objections highlight undercounting and the potential for a single large disaster to push totals higher; these risk factors support modest upward calibration.
Countervailing factors (seasonality, SAR capacity, policy constraints) keep the event far from certainty; thus probability remains uncertain but skewed upward.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections about undercounting and sudden disasters are valid and point to upside risk; pace data and threshold analysis support an upward bias, while weather/policy factors could dampen totals.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted probability from 0.54 to 0.60 to reflect the upward risk from undercounting and potential abrupt increases; kept range modest to reflect remaining uncertainty.

forecasts.reference-class: Historical Mediterranean migrant deaths per IOM Missing Migrants Project; typically around 2,000–2,500 deaths per calendar year, with monthly averages around 180; as of late Feb 2026 there were 606 deaths recorded in the Mediterranean through the first two months, suggesting two months remaining in April and potentially May with below/above-average risk.

causal-factors.name: Near-term pace of Mediterranean fatalities (Feb–Mar/Apr 2026) relative to annual baseline
causal-factors.rationale: As of late February 2026, 606 deaths have occurred; if the pace remains high into March–April, crossing 1,000 by end-April becomes more likely.

causal-factors.name: Remaining calendar window (March–April, with possible spill into May)
causal-factors.rationale: Two to three months remain in the window leading up to May, which adds significantly to the potential total if conditions stay adverse.

causal-factors.name: Historical annual fatality baseline on the Mediterranean
causal-factors.rationale: Historical totals in the low-to-mid thousands per year create a high upside potential if the current high pace persists.

causal-factors.name: Publicized record pace in early 2026 (media/UN/IOM emphasis)
causal-factors.rationale: Favorable coverage and warnings reflect and reinforce the perception of a risky environment with elevated cross-border mortality risk.

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and policy environment in the central Mediterranean
causal-factors.rationale: Improved SAR operations or policy measures could prevent deaths, reducing the probability of reaching 1,000 by May.

causal-factors.name: Potential for a major single shipwreck in March/April
causal-factors.rationale: A single catastrophe could add hundreds of deaths in a short period, sharply increasing the odds.

causal-factors.name: Unusually high early-2026 death pace (through February)
causal-factors.rationale: About 606 Mediterranean deaths had been recorded by Feb 24, 2026, indicating a record-pace start that would push the total toward 1,000 if that pace persists into March–April.

causal-factors.name: Unverified missing-person counts and reporting gaps
causal-factors.rationale: IOM notes substantial missing data and unverified tallies (e.g., thousands missing in 2025); if similar undercounting occurs in 2026, the risk of surpassing 1,000 by May increases.

causal-factors.name: Rescue capacity expansion (policy/financing increasing SAR)
causal-factors.rationale: Greater search-and-rescue capacity and funding could save more lives and dampen the death toll toward the end of April.

causal-factors.name: Policy/regulatory restrictions that limit SAR or crossing routes
causal-factors.rationale: Tighter border controls or reduced NGO/sar access can shrink rescue coverage and raise fatalities, increasing the odds of crossing the 1,000-death threshold.

causal-factors.name: Spring weather/sea-state conditions
causal-factors.rationale: Adverse spring seas and weather can increase hazard on Central Mediterranean crossings, elevating the risk of deaths.

causal-factors.name: Shifts in crossing patterns reducing Central Mediterranean traffic
causal-factors.rationale: Policy changes or shifts toward other routes (e.g., Canary Islands) could lower Central Mediterranean crossings and thus total deaths.

causal-factors.name: Pace of fatalities in early 2026 (through February)
causal-factors.rationale: With about 606 Mediterranean deaths (dead or missing) by the end of February, hitting 1,000 by the end of April would require roughly 197 deaths per month in March–April, i.e., a pace modestly above the historical monthly average (~180), making the outcome plausible but not assured.

causal-factors.name: Harsh weather and sea conditions in early 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Early 2026 saw severe weather including Cyclone Harry and related rough seas, which historically increases fatalities on the Central Mediterranean routes.

causal-factors.name: Surge in departures from Tunisia (Sfax) and central Mediterranean crossings
causal-factors.rationale: Reports of higher departures from Tunisia and dangerous crossings raise exposure and risk of fatalities, increasing the chance of rapidly accumulating deaths.

causal-factors.name: European policy tightening and border controls (Italy/EU)
causal-factors.rationale: Crackdowns on irregular migration and stricter asylum rules can suppress crossing flows, potentially reducing the number of deaths if fewer people attempt dangerous crossings.

causal-factors.name: Data gaps and potential undercount of fatalities
causal-factors.rationale: The Missing Migrants data are known to be incomplete in real time, so actual fatalities could exceed reported counts, nudging the eventual total higher.

synthesis: The existing ensemble sits near 0.54. Given a record early pace and plausible risk of sudden surges, a modest upward adjustment to around 0.60 is warranted, with a wide but bounded uncertainty range reflecting data gaps and potential countervailing factors.
